# Kanji Mode Decode Support for SkiaSharp.QrCode

## Purpose

This document defines the implementation order for reading ISO/IEC 18004 Kanji mode segments in all three symbologies (Standard QR, Micro QR, rMQR).

It defines WHAT is built, in WHICH order, and WHY. HOW each piece is verified follows the mandatory test-first workflow; fixture mechanics live in [QR Test Fixtures](../specs/qrcode-test-fixtures.md).

## Scope

**In scope.** Decoding Kanji mode segments: mode indicator `1000` (Standard QR), `100` (rMQR), `11` / `011` (Micro QR M3 / M4). Before this work all three decoders returned `QRCodeDecodeStatus.UnsupportedContent` for these segments, so symbols produced by Japanese-market encoders could not be read at all.

**Out of scope.** Kanji mode *encoding*. Emitting Kanji would change the default output of shipped generators for Japanese payloads, which is a separate compatibility decision. Decoding changes no output, so it is backward compatible and can ship on its own. This asymmetry (`Decode(Encode(x)) == x` holds; `Encode(Decode(y))` does not reproduce `y`) must be documented in the decoder specs.

**Also out of scope.** ECI 20 (Shift_JIS) byte-mode segments. They are adjacent (the divergence probe shows libzint emits exactly this for Japanese input) but need the full CP932 single-byte + double-byte range, roughly twice the table. Kanji mode is the narrower, higher-value target; ECI 20 stays a follow-up.

## Guiding Decisions

### The mapping is JIS X 0208, and that is a real choice

Kanji mode carries JIS X 0208 code points, but the JIS X 0208 standard mapping and Microsoft CP932 disagree about how a handful of them become Unicode. Getting this wrong produces a decoder that passes its own tests and mangles real-world symbols on exactly the characters (wave dash, minus sign, full-width currency signs) that Japanese payloads use most in URLs and price strings.

`probe-kanji-mapping` (2026-08-23) measured what each available oracle actually does, by encoding raw Shift_JIS bytes through qrtool (so no encoder-side mapping is involved) and reading the symbol back with two independent readers:

| Shift_JIS | zxing-cpp | ZXing.Net (.NET CP932) | Character |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0x815C | U+2015 | U+2015 | horizontal bar (agree) |
| 0x815F | **U+005C** | U+FF3C | reverse solidus vs fullwidth reverse solidus (found by the Phase 1 sweep, not by this probe) |
| 0x8160 | **U+301C** | U+FF5E | wave dash vs fullwidth tilde |
| 0x8161 | **U+2016** | U+2225 | double vertical line vs parallel to |
| 0x817C | **U+2212** | U+FF0D | minus sign vs fullwidth hyphen-minus |
| 0x8191 | **U+00A2** | U+FFE0 | cent sign |
| 0x8192 | **U+00A3** | U+FFE1 | pound sign |
| 0x81CA | **U+00AC** | U+FFE2 | not sign |

zxing-cpp applies the JIS X 0208 standard mapping; ZXing.Net inherits .NET's CP932. **We implement JIS X 0208**, so we agree with zxing-cpp and diverge from ZXing.Net on those cells.

The table above is the finished set of seven, but this probe found only six of them: the 0x815F row came out of the Phase 1 sweep, and 0x815C — which the usual "six divergent cells" folklore includes — turned out to agree. Note that Python's `shift_jis` codec is *not* a substitute reference: it matches this table on 8,022 of the 8,023 structurally valid cells and differs on exactly 0x815F, giving CP932's U+FF3C.

The consequence for tests is not optional: fixture payloads generated by ZXing.Net must stay clear of the divergent cells, and the divergent cells get their own qrtool fixture whose expected text is the JIS X 0208 reading.

### The table is derived, not transcribed, and independently verified

Hand-transcribing ~7,000 mappings is not reviewable. This section originally proposed generating from .NET CP932 plus an override list and verifying against zxing-cpp; Phase 1 inverted it, because the sweep turned out to be the better source. **The values come from the sweep** (qrtool encode into a zxing-cpp read, over every structurally valid cell), and **CP932 is the gate**: the generator refuses to emit unless the swept data reproduces JIS X 0208's published totals and its delta against CP932 is exactly the documented divergence set. Provenance is a reviewable measurement plus an independent arithmetic check, rather than a transcription anybody has to trust.

### One shared table, one shared decoder, three call sites

Kanji-mode compaction is symbology-independent: subtract 0x8140 (or 0xC140 for the upper range), then `msb × 0xC0 + lsb`, yielding exactly 13 bits. A single 8192-entry `ushort` table (**16,384 bytes**) covers the whole space with a direct index and no arithmetic on the happy path.

The three symbologies already carry their own Kanji character-count-indicator tables and their bit-stream loops already dispatch on the mode indicator, so each one needs a table lookup, a shared payload decoder, and one replaced `case` label. Doing all three at once costs barely more than doing rMQR alone, and Standard QR is where the interop hole actually hurts.

### Cost accepted, and why

- **+16 KB in every target framework** (~5% of the 343 KB net10.0 assembly, ~6% of netstandard2.0). Accepted: a `ReadOnlySpan<byte>` literal lands in RVA data, so there is no allocation and no static constructor, and the cost is a fixed per-process constant rather than anything that scales with input. A trimming feature switch is deliberately **not** built now; it is noted as a follow-up if the Blazor WASM payload becomes a concern.
- **No new dependencies.** `System.Text.Encoding.CodePages` is used by the fixture tool only. The library must not gain it: it is a real package on non-Windows, and the whole point of the table is to avoid it.
- **Runtime cost is negligible**, and `GetMaxDecodedLength` needs no change: Kanji spends 13 bits per character against Numeric's ~3.33, so the existing numeric-derived bound stays a strict upper bound.

### Unassigned cells fail loudly, they do not become U+FFFD

The Kanji-mode range is wider than JIS X 0208: 0xEAA5–0xEBBF is assigned by neither JIS X 0208 nor CP932, and 4 of every 192 index slots are structurally impossible (trail byte outside 0x40–0xFC minus 0x7F). Silently emitting a replacement character would turn a corrupt symbol into a plausible-looking wrong answer, which is the failure mode this library treats as worse than a rejection.

Table entry `0` marks "not mapped" (U+0000 is never a legitimate JIS X 0208 mapping). On a zero hit the decoder distinguishes the two causes and reports accordingly: a structurally impossible pair is `InvalidBitstream`, an unassigned but well-formed cell is `UnsupportedContent`. The distinguishing arithmetic sits on the error path only, so the happy path stays a single indexed load.

## Oracle Findings (probe results, 2026-08-23)

Recorded here because they overturn two assumptions in the existing fixture spec.

| Oracle | Standard QR | Micro QR | rMQR | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| ZXing.Net 0.16.11 | **Kanji encode** | - | - | `CHARACTER_SET = Shift_JIS` + all-double-byte input makes `chooseMode` return `KANJI`; the encoder self-reports the mode, so the fixture manifest does not need a reader to confirm it. Requires `CodePagesEncodingProvider` registered in the tool. Uses CP932, so payloads must avoid the seven divergent cells |
| qrtool 0.13.2 | **Kanji encode** | **Kanji encode** | **Kanji encode** | `--mode kanji` exists for every variant (the fixture spec's claim that it does not is wrong, corrected in Phase 1). Input must be raw **Shift_JIS bytes via `--read-from`**; UTF-8 input fails with "invalid character". Correctly rejects `--mode kanji` for M1/M2, which have no Kanji mode |
| libzint (via ZXingCpp) | no | no | no | `From(string)` rejects every non-ASCII input ("Error 245: Invalid UTF-8 in input"), a wrapper marshalling defect. `From(byte[])` **does** work and was previously unknown, but libzint then emits **Byte mode + ECI 20**, not Kanji: the symbol sizes match byte-count capacity exactly (46 kanji → R17x99 / v5-L, one version above the Kanji-mode fit). Usable later for ECI 20 fixtures, not for Kanji |
| zxing-cpp reader | read | read | read | Applies JIS X 0208. For a Kanji segment `Bytes` holds the **raw Shift_JIS bytes**, not UTF-8, so the sanity gate must compare against Shift_JIS bytes for these fixtures |

## Implementation Order

Priority is by interop value, not by symbology size: Standard QR first because that is what Japanese-market encoders actually emit, and because it is the only symbology with two independent Kanji oracles.

### Phase 1, oracle sweep and table generation

Blocking: every later phase asserts against this table.

- Extend the probe to sweep **every structurally valid Kanji-mode cell** through qrtool encode → zxing-cpp decode, chunked across v40-L symbols.
- Diff the sweep against .NET CP932; the divergence set becomes the override list. Resolve the open question of NEC row 13 (0x8740–0x879C), assigned by CP932, unassigned by JIS X 0208, from what the sweep shows.
- Generate `ShiftJisKanjiTable` into `src/` from CP932 + overrides; re-run the sweep as a verification pass that must reach 100%.
- Correct the qrtool Kanji claim in the fixture spec and record the oracle matrix updates.

### Phase 2, shared decode path and Standard QR

- Red: a `SegmentDecoders` unit test for `DecodeKanjiPayload` covering both ranges, the divergent cells, unassigned cells, and structurally impossible pairs (negative cases at least matching positive cases in count, per the decode-acceptance rule).
- Green: `ShiftJisKanjiTable` lookup + `SegmentDecoders.DecodeKanjiPayload`; replace the `case ModeKanji` return in `QRBinaryDecoder`. Standard QR keeps returning `UnsupportedContent` for FNC1 and Structured Append, which the spec wording must not blur.
- Fixtures: ZXing.Net Kanji lineage (payloads free of divergent cells) plus a qrtool Standard QR Kanji lineage including a divergent-cell case.

### Phase 3, Micro QR

- Wire `MicroQRBinaryDecoder`, whose `modeValue > ModeKanji` guard already reserves the indicator. M3 and M4 only.
- Fixtures: qrtool Kanji cases for M3/M4 at each legal ECC level, plus a negative expectation that M1/M2 cannot carry Kanji.

### Phase 4, rMQR

- Wire `RmQRBinaryDecoder`.
- Fixtures: qrtool Kanji cases spanning heights and both ECC levels.

### Phase 5, specs, size and performance record

- Update `standardqr-decoder.md`, `rmqr-decoder.md`, the Micro QR decoder scope, `qrcode-symbologies.md` (Kanji scope decision changes from "deferred" to "decode-only"), `docs/data-capacity.md`, and the root README.
- Record the measured assembly-size delta per TFM and confirm decode benchmarks stay within +10% mean and allocated.

## Working Rules

- Test-first is mandatory for every `src/` change: failing test, then implementation, then full suite on net8.0 and net10.0.
- Fixture regeneration is an explicit reviewed commit; the corpus exists to make encoder drift visible.
- Progress logging (mandatory): when a phase completes, append an entry to the Progress log below recording what was done, lessons learned, and benchmark deltas, or an explicit statement of why benchmarks are not applicable.

## Progress log

### Phase 1, oracle sweep and table generation, completed 2026-08-23

**Done**

- `probe-kanji`, `probe-kanji-mapping` and `probe-kanji-sweep` added to `tools/QRInteropFixtures`. The sweep pushes all 8,023 structurally valid Kanji-mode cells through qrtool (raw Shift_JIS bytes) into the zxing-cpp reader and diffs the result against .NET CP932; `kanji-sweep.tsv` is committed as the provenance record.
- `generate-kanji-table` emits `src/SkiaSharp.QrCode/Internals/ShiftJisKanjiTable.cs` (8,192 × `ushort` = 16,384 bytes, little-endian byte literal so it lands in RVA data). It refuses to write unless the swept data satisfies JIS X 0208's published totals and its CP932 delta is exactly the documented divergence set.
- **Regenerating the table changes a golden digest.** `ShiftJisKanjiTableUnitTest.Table_MatchesItsGoldenDigest` hashes all 8,192 entries, because every other table test constrains only WHICH cells are assigned and would pass a table whose readings were permuted. The generator prints the new digest on every run; paste it into `GoldenDigest` in that test as part of the same reviewed change.
- Fixture spec corrected: qrtool **does** have `--mode kanji`, for all three variants.

**Lessons learned**

- The sweep resolved every open question at once and overturned two guesses. The divergence set is **seven** cells, not the six that are usually quoted: 0x815F (reverse solidus U+005C vs fullwidth U+FF3C) was not on the list going in, and 0x815C, which was, turns out to agree (both U+2015). Guessing the override list from memory would have shipped two wrong cells.
- The strongest validation was arithmetic, not comparison: zxing-cpp assigns exactly **6,879** cells, which is JIS X 0208's published repertoire size (524 non-kanji + 6,355 kanji) to the character. That number, reproduced independently, is what makes "this really is JIS X 0208" a measurement rather than an assumption, and it is now the generator's gate.
- The NEC row 13 question (0x8740-0x879C: circled digits, unit ligatures, `㈱`) resolved cleanly against the sweep: CP932 assigns a character to 83 of the range's 92 structurally valid cells (it leaves 0x875E and 0x8776-0x877D unassigned too), zxing-cpp assigns none, and excluding them is what makes the total come out at 6,879. They stay unmapped, so a symbol carrying `①` in Kanji mode is reported as unsupported rather than decoded under a mapping the standard does not define.
- CP932 does not report unassigned cells as unmapped: .NET returns U+30FB for them, so a naive "did it decode?" filter counts 1,061 phantom assignments on top of the 83 real NEC row 13 characters. Any comparison against CP932 has to know that.
- The structural cell count falls out of the compaction arithmetic (42 lead values × 188 expressible trails + 127 for the capped last lead = 8,023) and matched the sweep exactly, which confirmed the enumeration before any table existed.

**Benchmarks**

- Not applicable: no `src/` change in this phase beyond adding the generated table, which nothing referenced yet.

### Phases 2-4, shared decode path and all three symbologies, completed 2026-08-23

**Done**

- `SegmentDecoders.DecodeKanjiPayload` (13 bits per character, bitstream sufficiency checked before destination sufficiency, matching the numeric and alphanumeric decoders).
- Wired into all three bitstream decoders. Count-indicator widths: `EncodingModeExtensions.GetKanjiCountIndicatorLength` (8/10/12 by version band), `MicroQRConstants.GetKanjiCountIndicatorLength` (M3 = 3, M4 = 4, throwing for M1/M2), and the existing `RmQRConstants.GetKanjiCountIndicatorLength`.
- Tests: `ShiftJisKanjiTableUnitTest` (checked against JIS X 0208's published totals and row/cell layout rather than against the generator's source), `SegmentDecodersKanjiUnitTest` (negative cases outnumbering positive), Kanji cases added to all three bitstream decoder suites, and `KanjiFixtureTest` as the explicit cross-symbology guarantee.
- Fixtures: 14 new externally generated Kanji symbols (5 Standard QR from ZXing.Net, 5 Micro QR M3/M4 and 4 rMQR from qrtool), all through their sanity gates. One rMQR case carries the seven divergent cells with its Shift_JIS bytes pinned.

**Deliberately not done**

- Phase 2 planned a **qrtool Standard QR lineage** alongside ZXing.Net, with the divergent-cell case there. Standard QR has only ever had one generator, so adding qrtool would mean a new `IFixtureGenerator` plus a second full 26-case Standard QR corpus, which is a fixture-infrastructure change rather than Kanji work. The divergent-cell case went into the qrtool rMQR lineage instead, where the generator already exists and the raw Shift_JIS bytes reach the encoder the same way. Standard QR therefore has one Kanji lineage, not two; adding qrtool for Standard QR remains worthwhile on its own merits.
- No trimming feature switch for the 16 KB table. Noted in the plan as a follow-up if the Blazor WASM payload becomes a concern; nothing measured yet says it is.

**Lessons learned**

- Doing all three symbologies together cost almost nothing over doing one. The table and payload decoder are shared, the count-indicator tables already existed, and each symbology needed one replaced `case` label. Standard QR, the one with the most real-world Kanji traffic, would have been the wrong one to leave for later.
- `UnsupportedContent` had been doing double duty. Kanji shared it with FNC1, Structured Append and unmapped ECI charsets, so the existing "Kanji is rejected" tests passed for a reason that had nothing to do with Kanji, and they kept passing after the wiring until the assertions were rewritten. A status that means several things cannot be used to prove any one of them.
- Splitting a zero lookup into two verdicts by structural validity is what keeps the failure honest: a value no Shift_JIS pair can express is `InvalidBitstream`, a well-formed cell outside the repertoire is `UnsupportedContent`. The distinguishing arithmetic sits on the error path, so the happy path stays one indexed load.
- ZXing.Net caches its Shift_JIS lookup in static initializers, so registering `CodePagesEncodingProvider` at the call site silently produced Byte mode instead of Kanji. It has to be registered before anything in the process encodes. The generator now fails loudly on the mode instead of writing a mislabelled fixture.
- Regenerating the corpus rewrote 400 unrelated fixture files with different line endings and no content change, exactly as the fixture spec warns. `git diff --ignore-cr-at-eol` confirmed the churn and the files were restored rather than committed.

**Benchmarks**

- See Phase 5.

**Adversarial review, completed 2026-08-23**

Seven rounds of independent reviewers plus refutation votes, run after the phases above. It changed one thing in the shipped decode path — the Micro QR restructure described below — and otherwise added tests and corrected documents.

- **Every defect it found in the implementation was a missing test, not wrong logic.** The correctness pass came back empty twice, once behind 76.5 M differential cases. What the rounds actually found was five unpinned things: the Standard QR 12-bit Kanji count band (deleting it passed the whole suite), the 6,879 table values (only the assignment *pattern* was tested, so a permutation passed), the rMQR truncated-count guard, the exact-fill boundary in `DecodeKanjiPayload`, and the Kanji-then-another-segment continuation in two decoders.
- **The tests that hid the gaps were shaped wrong, not absent.** The Micro QR negative cases passed a raw bit length as `dataBitCount`, leaving the buffer LONGER than the capacity — the inverse of production. `BitReader` bounds itself on the buffer, so a decoder with the capacity check deleted read pad bits quietly instead of throwing, and the test that existed specifically to guard that throw could not fail. **A negative test on a parser has to reproduce production's buffer-vs-bound relationship, or it tests nothing.**
- **rMQR and Micro QR gained the fuzz test Standard QR already had.** That single pre-existing test was the only thing protecting the Standard QR equivalent of the rMQR guard. Structural defences do not transfer to a new symbology on their own.
- **The last gap it found predated this work, and closing it properly meant widening the fix.** The bit-sufficiency guard in `DecodeKanjiPayload` was pinned from above (exact fill must succeed) but not from below (one bit short must fail) — and the same was true of the numeric, alphanumeric and byte decoders beside it. `SegmentDecoderCapacityBoundaryTest` now pins all four from both sides. Numeric and alphanumeric needed a third dimension to be pinnable at all: they re-check per group inside their loops, so weakening the up-front guard is invisible until the destination is also short, at which point the status flips from `InvalidBitstream` to `DestinationTooSmall` and a caller is told to grow a buffer instead of that the symbol is malformed.
- **Two reviewer claims were wrong and had to be refuted rather than acted on.** One recommended hoisting Kanji out of the Micro QR switch to a spot that skips the truncated-count check; a differential run found 482 `InvalidOperationException`s escaping a `bool`-returning `TryDecode`. Another reported a surviving mutant (`if (count == 0) break;` inside a `switch` case) whose effect it had misread — `break` leaves the switch, not the loop, so the mutant is equivalent and proves nothing. **A surviving mutant is evidence only once you exhibit an input where it differs.**

**Decode benchmarks**

Both sides measured at `--warmupCount 5 --iterationCount 15`, baseline built from a `git worktree` at the pre-change commit. Allocation is unchanged everywhere (the table is RVA data, the payload decoder allocates nothing).

Final state, 20 iterations, against a baseline built from the pre-change commit and measured at the same settings:

| Class | Worst regression | Worst improvement |
|---|---|---|
| `QRCodeDecodeEndToEnd` | +3.9 % (`QR_Byte_V40_L`) | −2.9 % (`QR_Byte_V40_H (Span)`) |
| `RmQRDecodeEndToEnd` | +1.6 % (`RmQR_Byte_R17x139`) | −2.6 % (`RmQR_Alphanumeric_R11x59`) |
| `MicroQRDecodeEndToEnd` | +3.3 % (`Byte_M4`) | −5.1 % (`Alphanumeric_M3 (Span)`) |

Everything is inside the ±10 % guardrail and allocation is unchanged on every row. The Micro QR figures are post-review: the first shipped shape regressed the allocating `Numeric_M2` and `Byte_M4` by 12-15 %, which the review caught and the restructure below removed (301.8 / 579.4 ns against a 305.9 / 561.1 ns baseline).

**Lessons learned**

- `MicroQR_Numeric_M2_Decode` and `MicroQR_Byte_M4_Decode` in their allocating overloads were **a real +12 % / +15 % regression**, and the first two rounds of investigation wrongly wrote it off as measurement spread. The misleading signal was that the allocation-free twins of the same payloads were flat or faster in the same runs, which looked like proof that the shared decode path had not changed. It was not proof: the cost landed only on the allocating overloads, so comparing the twins pointed the wrong way.
- **What settled it was a three-way bisect measured back to back**: baseline, HEAD with only `MicroQRBinaryDecoder` reverted, and full HEAD. The middle build sat exactly on baseline (300.7 vs 305.9, 561.9 vs 561.1) while full HEAD was 336.8 / 645.6. One file, unambiguously. Interleaving the three in one session is what made intervals of ±2-6 ns trustworthy; earlier A/B pairs taken hours apart had drifted enough to hide it.
- The payload `switch` is where it came from: adding a fourth arm takes Roslyn past its jump-table threshold, and the shipped shape emits no `switch` instruction at all while the four-arm shape emits one with three targets (verified in IL on all four TFMs). Whether the jump table itself is what costs the time is NOT established — an isolated micro-benchmark of the dispatch shows only noise, and `DecodeBitStream` is under a quarter of the benchmark it moved, so code layout is at least as likely. The shape is measured-better, not explained. The fix is to handle Kanji in an `if` **after** the shared truncated-count and zero-count rules and **before** the switch, which leaves the switch at its original three arms. Placing that `if` *earlier* — the obvious-looking spot next to the count-width branch — is a live defect: it skips the truncated-count check, and `BitReader` then throws `InvalidOperationException` out of a `bool`-returning `TryDecode`. A differential run over 1.6 M random bitstreams found 482 such throws.
- `DecodeKanjiPayload` had been marked `NoInlining` to "protect the callers' inlining budget", but the callers are 353-514 IL bytes and were never inline candidates. The attribute was removed. **An unmeasured performance rationale written into a comment is worse than no comment: the next reader takes it as an established invariant, and here it also masked the real regression sitting three lines away.**
